corrections.source_says: Keep core=no and context_class=observational, but revise the explanation that the fit is borderline because creativity or idea novelty was not rated. Under the supplied codebook, computed diversity of real papers across time is sufficient for observational context. The field-level topic Gini and cross-field dispersion measures directly provide that evidence. The absence of random assignment excludes the paper from the core and two-screener randomized-people pipeline; it does not make these collective-diversity outcomes ineligible as observational context.

confirmed: Read the entire markdown, including references and all supplementary material. The PDF has 46 pages and identifies arXiv:2607.20923v1 [cs.DL], 23 Jul 2026; the title and four authors match the form (PDF p. 1).
The supplement occupies PDF pp. 22-46, numbered S1-S25, and includes Notes 1-2, Figures S1-S13, and Tables S1-S4 (PDF pp. 22 and 46).

Both datasets are observational, with no people assigned to AI assistance. The randomized within-paper baseline reshuffles existing contribution roles; it is not a human experiment. Core exclusion is correct, and no small randomized experiment or synthesis is present (PDF pp. 3, 12, 14-17).

The first dataset contains 775,323 seed authors, from 3,959,771 candidates. The exclusions of papers with more than 20 authors and the top 2% of candidate authors, and both minimum-three-publication requirements, match the form (PDF p. 15, Data).
The Data section reports 26,057,772 works and 18,499,462 distinct coauthors across the seed authors publication histories; these are not additional randomized participants (PDF p. 15).
China accounts for 27.2% and the United States for 14.8% of seed authors, not the collaborator percentages (PDF p. 43/S22, Table S2).

The Results print 244,062 high-AI-writing authors and 211,911 low-AI-writing authors before describing annual matching; the matched contrast participant count is not supplied (PDF pp. 6, 16-17; Table S4, p. 45/S24).

The second dataset has 137,120 multi-author papers: 128,613 PLOS and 8,507 other PMC papers, with 945,989 paper-author observations after excluding 2,683 solo-authored papers. Its distinct-person count is not stated, so n_analyzed=null is appropriate (PDF p. 15, Data).
The author panel analyzes 2011-2025; the contribution-role data cover 2018-2025 and use 14 CRediT categories (PDF p. 24/S3, Note 2; p. 15, Data; p. 41/S20, Table S1).
S1-O1 matches the Results: Rao-Stirling 0.176 in 2022 to 0.199 in 2025, 13.0% above trend; distinct fields 2.3 to 2.8, 15.6% above trend; Shannon entropy 0.55 to 0.71 (PDF p. 3; Fig. 1a-c, p. 4).
S1-O2 matches the Results: 35.5% entered at least one new field in 2025 versus 30.4% in 2022, with the 2025 level 23.2% above the extrapolated trend (PDF p. 3; Fig. 1d, p. 4).

S1-O3 matches the Results: pivot size 0.236 in 2011, 0.226 in 2022, and 0.242 in 2025. Pivot is cosine distance from the previous three publication years reference-field profile, averaged across eligible papers per author (PDF pp. 5 and 16).

S1-O4 numerical transcription matches p. 6: r=0.237 and r=0.230, both p<0.001; 0.143 and 0.230 for the stated AI-writing-rate means; 0.172 and 0.295 for the stated pivot sizes. Decile definitions and contrast attribution need the corrections above (PDF pp. 6-7).

S1-O5 accurately reproduces the main-text claim that Gini declined across over 3,000 topics; the caption specifies 3,731 topics. Exact Gini endpoint estimates are not printed (PDF p. 5; Fig. S6a and caption, pp. 32-33/S11-S12).

Figures 1 and 2 specify 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The event-study models use author-year observations, author-clustered standard errors, and a 2022 reference year; Figures S5 and S9 show 95% intervals (PDF pp. 4, 7, 24/S3, 31/S10, 36/S15).

AI exposure is a writing-pattern proxy, not observed tool use: the estimator uses a human/AI sentence-distribution mixture and maximum likelihood with bioRxiv word probabilities (PDF p. 14, Limitations; pp. 23-24/S2-S3, Note 1).

The one-line finding matches the printed author count, Rao-Stirling values and trend comparison, new-field shares, and pre-existing then widening high/low group gaps; it is descriptive rather than causal (PDF pp. 3, 6, 15).

Leaving S2 without eligible creativity/diversity outcomes is appropriate: its similarity measure compares reported contributor role sets rather than creative outputs (PDF pp. 10 and 17, Pairwise Role-Set Similarity).
summary: The full arXiv v1 supports observational context evidence, with no randomized people study, and the recorded headline numbers match the PDF. Corrections concern matched-comparison labeling, source inconsistencies, omitted outcomes, and the coding and description of collective diversity.
